newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - Countries mull who owns future cure for cancer.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Countries mull who owns future cure for cancer.

text.p: Rain forests, coral reefs, geysers and other exotic environments may well harbour the cure for cancer, AIDS or other diseases, waiting to be discovered. The question facing international negotiators is, who will own it?

Indigenous peoples who first used particular medicinal plants, landowners, countries where new drugs may be found, and international pharmaceuticals companies poised to develop and market them have staked conflicting "bioprospecting" claims, and lawyers are trying to sort them out.

Germany is on the regulatory forefront pushing for a resolution of the tangled issue, as it is home to some of the world's biggest drug companies like Hoechst AG and Bayer AG, and is the second-largest importer of plant-based drugs after Hong Kong.
Bioprospecting is the painstaking process of sifting through the genetic material of little-known life forms for substances that may be used in medicines or industry.

The thorny issue of conflicting claims is addressed by the Convention on Biological Diversity floated at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro. The convention took effect in 1993 and has been ratified by nearly 160 countries.
But negotiators are only now getting down to the fundamentals of implementing the convention in national law.

Parties to the biodiversity convention will gather in Buenos Aires in November to discuss how best to regulate access to genetic resources and divide benefits, a sensitive issue between the developed countries of the North and developing countries of the South.

"What we are concerned about is the fair and equitable sharing of benefits derived from genetic resources, to define a new relationship between providers and users," said Lyle Glowka, a Bonn-based lawyer for the IUCN-World Conservation Union, which drew up an early draft of the convention.
Environmentalists estimate only 5,000 of the world's 250,000 plant species have been thoroughly screened for their therapeutic potential.

Germany has a master plan for implementing the convention, and is developing models that include combinations of up-front payments, royalties, technology transfer and repatriation of research, said Marc Auer, a conservation specialist at the Environment Ministry.
"We are relatively progressive on this issue," Auer said.

Ultimately, the success of the plan will rest on voluntary commitments by industry, as it is practically impossible to control international traffic in plant substances, let alone micro-organisms, he said.
Historically, drug companies had no obligation to share benefits from new drugs with the country where the active ingredient originated.

In the famous case of the rosy periwinkle, Eli Lilly paid nothing to Madagascar for a rare plant found there that led to the development of cancer treatments that produce annual revenues of more than $100 million.

Poorer countries in Asia, Africa and South America now hope to get a greater share of the benefits for themselves, perhaps by becoming partners in developing drugs instead of mere vendors of genetic samples.
Drug companies hope the talks will guarantee them continued and exclusive access to the exotic plants, animals and especially micro-organisms that may yield the wonder drugs of the future.

And conservationists hope to put safeguards in place to keep the two sides from simply declaring open season on the fragile and unexploited environments that are seen as offering the biggest potential for yielding useful medicines.

Under a pact concluded in 1992 and seen as a model, Merck & Co of the U.S. agreed to pay Costa Rica's National Biodiversity Institute (INBio) for samples of medicinal plants, putting up $1.3 million for laboratory equipment and an undisclosed percentage of royalties from any future medicines that might be developed.
INBio has since reached similar agreements with other drug makers, but terms have not been disclosed.

"We see the INBio-Merck agreement as a positive model, and we would be prepared to deal with other countries on a similar basis," said Dieter Berg, a specialist in international cooperation on plant protection at Bayer.
"The money is a realistic sum, and INBio has a government mandate to negotiate. Other aspects of the current talks, however, are raising expectations too high," he said.
Trade in botanical samples is not easily regulated by the state, and would best be handled in direct negotiations between companies and countries of origin, Berg said.
"There is no sense in making things so formal," he said. INBio has been succesful with U.S. companies, though the U.S. has not ratified the treaty, he added.
